parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the reason why two objects that are at the same temperature are described as being in thermal equilibrium.

markscheme_points.text: no net thermal energy is transferred (between them)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what would happen if two objects at different temperatures are put in contact - in which direction does thermal energy flow, and when does that flow stop?
parts.proper_answer: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium because there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Temperature Really Means**
Think of temperature as telling you which way thermal energy wants to flow. If one object is hotter, energy flows from hot to cold. If both are at the same temperature, there is no driving force for a net flow either way.

Step 2: **Link to Thermal Equilibrium**
So being in thermal equilibrium does not mean no energy moves at all at the microscopic level, it means the flows balance. The correct statement is that the net rate of thermal energy transfer between them is zero.

Fig. 3.1 shows the variations with temperature of the densities of mercury and of water between $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $100^{\circ}\text{C}$.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1

Temperature may be measured using the variation with temperature of the density of a liquid.

Suggest why, for measuring temperature over this temperature range:

markscheme_points.text: variation (of density with temperature) is linear or each temperature has a unique value of density

hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the shape of the mercury density-temperature graph in Fig. 3.1 - what is special about a straight-line graph for making a scale?
parts.proper_answer: For mercury the density varies linearly with temperature, so each value of density corresponds to one unique temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Makes a Good Thermometer**
A good thermometric property must change steadily and predictably with temperature, so that every temperature gives a different reading and you can calibrate evenly spaced marks.

Step 2: **Apply to Mercury**
The mercury graph in Fig. 3.1 is a straight line falling gently from $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$. That linear fall means density is a suitable property because each temperature has a unique density value.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: water is not a suitable liquid.

markscheme_points.text: variation (of density with temperature) is not linear
region where the density does not vary with temperature
different temperatures have the same density

hints: Hint 1: Compare the water graph shape to the mercury straight line - where does it go flat or turn over near $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to about $4^{\circ}\text{C}$?
Hint 2: Think about what happens if two different temperatures give exactly the same density reading - could you tell which temperature you have?
parts.proper_answer: Water is unsuitable because its density variation is non-linear, there is a region where density hardly changes with temperature, and different temperatures can have the same density.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Problem Shape**
Look at the water graph. It rises slightly then falls with a curve. It is not a straight line, so the change in density per degree is not constant.

Step 2: **Two Fatal Flaws for a Thermometer**
First, near the maximum the curve is almost flat, so density hardly varies with temperature and sensitivity is very poor. Second, because it goes up then down, the same density value occurs at two different temperatures, so the reading is not unique and you cannot tell which temperature it is.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A beaker contains a liquid of mass $120\text{ g}$. The liquid is supplied with thermal energy at a rate of $810\text{ W}$. The beaker has a mass of $42\text{ g}$ and a specific heat capacity of $0.84\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. The beaker and the liquid are in thermal equilibrium with each other at all times and are insulated from the surroundings.

Fig. 3.2 shows the variation with time $t$ of the temperature of the liquid.

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

Fig. 3.2
parts.text: State the boiling temperature, in $^{\circ}\text{C}$, of the liquid.
hints: Hint 1: On the temperature-time graph in Fig. 3.2, find where the temperature stops rising even though heating continues - what does that flat section tell you?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading a Heating Curve**
When a liquid is heated it warms up, then boils. During boiling all the supplied energy goes into breaking bonds, not raising temperature, so the graph becomes horizontal.

Step 2: **Read the Plateau Value**
In Fig. 3.2 the straight rise from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ stops at $21\text{ s}$ and then stays flat. Reading across to the temperature axis gives $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. That is the boiling point.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: On the temperature-time graph in Fig. 3.2, find where the temperature stops rising even though heating continues - what does that flat section tell you?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading a Heating Curve**

Step 2: **Read the Plateau Value**

marking_points.text: boiling point = 80 °C

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the specific heat capacity, in $\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, of the liquid.

markscheme_points.text: thermal energy absorbed by beaker = 42 × 0.84 × (80 − 25) (= 1940 J)

hints: Hint 1: Start by identifying from Fig. 3.2 how long the warming-up stage lasts and what the temperature rise is - the supplied energy is shared between liquid and beaker.
Hint 2: Think about how to find the total energy delivered by the heater from power and time, and separately the energy that warms the beaker.
Hint 3: Recall how energy, mass, temperature change and specific heat capacity are linked for both the beaker and the liquid.
Hint 4: Remember to subtract the beaker energy from the total to leave only the energy heating the liquid, then rearrange to find $c$ and check units of $\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: Total supplied $Q = 810 \times 21 = 1.7 \times 10^{4}\text{ J}$, beaker absorbs $42 \times 0.84 \times 55 = 1940\text{ J}$, so $c = 2.3\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the Time and Temperature Rise**
You are heating from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ to boiling at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. So $$\Delta \theta = 80 - 25 = 55\text{ K}$$ The rise ends at $t = 21\text{ s}$ from Fig. 3.2. A common mistake is to use $60\text{ s}$ - only the sloping part is warming.

Step 2: **Total Energy Supplied**
Power is energy per second, so $$Q_{total} = Pt$$ $$Q_{total} = 810 \times 21 = 17010\text{ J}$$ This warms both liquid and beaker, which stay in thermal equilibrium together.

Step 3: **Energy Taken by the Beaker**
The beaker also warms by $55\text{ K}$: $$Q_{beaker} = m_{b}c_{b}\Delta\theta$$ $$Q_{beaker} = 42 \times 0.84 \times 55 = 1940\text{ J}$$ You must not forget this - otherwise you overestimate $c$ of the liquid.

Step 4: **Find c of the Liquid**
Energy left for liquid: $$Q_{liquid} = Q_{total} - Q_{beaker}$$ $$c = \frac{Q_{liquid}}{m\Delta\theta} = \frac{(810 \times 21) - (42 \times 0.84 \times 55)}{120 \times 55}$$ $$c = 2.3\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$ to 2 s.f. Note masses are in $\text{g}$ so $c$ comes out per gram, as required.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
The experiment in (c) is repeated using water instead of the liquid in (c). The mass of liquid used, the power supplied, and the initial temperature are all unchanged.
The specific heat capacity of water is approximately twice that of the liquid in (c).
The boiling temperature of water is $100^{\circ}\text{C}$.

On Fig. 3.2, sketch the variation with time $t$ of the temperature of the water between $t = 0$ and $t = 60\text{ s}$. Numerical calculations are not required.

markscheme_points.text: sketch: straight diagonal line from 25 °C to 100 °C and then horizontal
straight diagonal line starting at 25 °C with gradient approximately half

hints: Hint 1: Think about what twice the specific heat capacity means for the rate of temperature rise if power and mass are the same - faster or slower?
Hint 2: Consider where the new line must start, what its slope is compared to the old line, and where it must level off for water boiling at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$.
parts.proper_answer: Sketch a straight line starting at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ with about half the gradient of the original, rising to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ then horizontal to $t = 60\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Slower Warming**
For the same $P$, $\Delta\theta / \Delta t = P / (mc)$. Larger $c$ means smaller gradient. Water has about twice the $c$, so the temperature rises about half as fast. Start at the same $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ at $t = 0$ with a shallower straight line.

Step 2: **Higher Plateau**
Water boils at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, not $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. So continue the shallow line up to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ and then draw it horizontal, showing boiling at constant temperature. It reaches $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ much later than $21\text{ s}$, near the end of the $60\text{ s}$ interval.

key_concepts: effect of larger specific heat capacity on heating rate
gradient inversely proportional to heat capacity
